transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Israeli election officials will soon finish counting ballots from yesterday's election.
NPR's Daniel Estrin reports there's no clear winner yet.
"The majority of votes have been counted, but the race is still in a deadlock.
We do not know who will be declared the next prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu or Gadi
Eisenkot, his center-right challenger.
For now, it looks like Eisenkot will have the support of the majority of lawmakers voted
now into parliament, and that is thanks to what looks like a historically strong performance
by Arab-led parties.
They want Eisenkot to be the next prime minister.
However, it is really unclear and quite unlikely that Eisenkot's camp would actually be willing
to form a coalition with Arab parties."
NPR's Daniel Estrin reporting.
In the U.S., the state of Alaska is asking a judge to immediately dismiss a Justice Department
lawsuit.
The suit would block election results if incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan narrowly loses
to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin reports.
The case involves a third candidate on the ballot, also named Dan Sullivan.
The Justice Department says voter confusion could taint the election and wants an investigation
if the senator loses, but would have won if votes for both Sullivans were counted for
him.
Election law experts say the case is unusually weak, based entirely on a law that governs
voter registration, not ballot issues.
The state's defense wasn't a given since it tried to boot the challenger from the ballot
this summer.
Now, the state says the lawsuit has no legal basis and that the ballot clearly differentiates
the two Sullivans.
One is identified as the Republican incumbent.
For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage.
The midterm elections are now less than a week away.
New data show some Americans are turning to AI chatbots for help in deciding how to vote.
NPR's Windsor Johnston has more.
A new study by the Pew Research Center finds 8 percent of American adults use AI chatbots
for midterm election information.
Among that group, 40 percent seek suggestions about how to vote.
But those answers can contain misinformation.
Boston University communications professor Michelle Amazin says even citing a familiar
news organization or polling group doesn't guarantee accuracy.
If you're using an AI chatbot to fact check political claims, you should prompt it for
its sources and go to those sources to make sure that it's not hallucinating.
Amazin also warns that answers that feel right just because they match your beliefs aren't
necessarily accurate.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Officials in Spain say that at least 64 people have now died after a train collided with
the second one today that was stopped on the tracks for unknown reasons.
Authorities fear the death toll will continue to rise.
Spanish government officials suggest that human error is the cause of today's accident,
but no official reason has been released.
Leaders from across Africa are gathering in Moscow for a two-day summit hosted by Russian
President Vladimir Putin.
As NPR's Charles Mayne's reports from the Russian capital, the event signals Russia's
growing ambitions on the African continent.
This is the third Russia-Africa summit Putin has hosted since 2019, and according to the
Kremlin, dignitaries from nearly 50 African countries, including 22 heads of state, will
be on hand for the event.
The summit comes amid wider Russian efforts to deepen its political, economic and military
partnerships with African nations.
But even as Russian trade in energy and agriculture has expanded, deals have not always kept up
with declarations, and African countries will be seeking to lock down promised Russian investments
or look elsewhere.
Meanwhile, for the Kremlin, the summit serves a more immediate purpose, showing Russia is
far from isolated despite Western sanctions over its war in Ukraine.
Charles Mayne's NPR News, Moscow.
Officials in India say Cyclone Arnab has killed at least three people.
The cyclone made landfall earlier today before losing strength and pushing inland.
Forecasters say the cyclone is expected to continue weakening and will dissipate by tomorrow.
This is NPR.
This message comes from Angie.

topics.text: Israeli election officials near final ballot count, with no clear winner between Netanyahu and Eisenkot
Alaska asks judge to dismiss Justice Department lawsuit over Sullivan ballot confusion in Senate race
Survey finds 8 percent of U.S. adults use AI chatbots for midterm election information
Spain train collision kills at least 64 people after collision with a stopped train
Russian President Putin hosts Russia-Africa summit in Moscow with dozens of African leaders
Cyclone Arnab makes landfall in India, killing at least three people before weakening inland
